title: Research
text:
My research focuses on using numerical models and machine learning methods to better understand complex physical processes like how glaciers flow or fires spread over the landscape. Much of my work has focused on glaciology, particularly looking at how glaciers and ice sheets respond to changes in climate.

Selected publications


[1] L. Zeller, D. McGrath, L. Sass, C. Florentine, and J. Downs, “Equilibrium line altitudes, accumulation areas and the vulnerability of glaciers in alaska,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 71, p. e28, Jan. 2025, doi: 10.1017/jog.2024.65.


[2] A. A. Marcozzi, J. V. Johnson, R. A. Parsons, S. J. Flanary, C. A. Seielstad, and J. Z. Downs, “Application of LiDAR derived fuel cells to wildfire modeling at laboratory scale,” Fire, vol. 6, no. 10, p. 394, Oct. 2023, doi: 10.3390/fire6100394.


[3] J. Downs and J. V. Johnson, “A rapidly retreating, marine-terminating glacier’s modeled response to perturbations in basal traction,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 68, no. 271, pp. 891–900, Oct. 2022, doi: 10.1017/jog.2022.5.


[4] J. P. Briner et al., “Rate of mass loss from the greenland ice sheet will exceed holocene values this century,” Nature, vol. 586, no. 7827, pp. 70–74, Oct. 2020, doi: 10.1038/s41586-020-2742-6.


[5] J. Z. Downs, J. V. Johnson, J. T. Harper, T. Meierbachtol, and M. A. Werder, “Dynamic hydraulic conductivity reconciles mismatch between modeled and observed winter subglacial water pressure,” Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, vol. 123, no. 4, pp. 818–836, 2018, doi: 10.1002/2017JF004522.


[6] B. D. Fleurian et al., “SHMIP the subglacial hydrology model intercomparison project,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 64, no. 248, pp. 897–916, Dec. 2018, doi: 10.1017/jog.2018.78.


[7] J. Downs, D. Brinkerhoff, and M. Morlighem, “Inferring time-dependent calving dynamics at helheim glacier,” Journal of Glaciology, vol. 69, no. 274, pp. 381–396, Apr. 2023, doi: 10.1017/jog.2022.68.


[8] J. Downs, J. Johnson, J. Briner, N. Young, A. Lesnek, and J. Cuzzone, “Western greenland ice sheet retreat history reveals elevated precipitation during the holocene thermal maximum,” The Cryosphere, vol. 14, no. 3, pp. 1121–1137, Mar. 2020, doi: 10.5194/tc-14-1121-2020.

title: WARP.md
text:
This file provides guidance to WARP (warp.dev) when working with code in this repository.


This is an academic portfolio website built with Quarto and hosted on GitHub Pages. It contains research publications, teaching materials, blog posts, and personal information for Jacob Downs, an assistant professor at the University of Montana.






Root level: Main pages (index, research, teaching, about) as .qmd files
posts/: Blog posts and writing, with each post as a dated .qmd file

_metadata.yml: Default formatting configuration for all posts
index.qmd: Auto-generates listing page from post contents

**_site/**: Generated static site output (gitignored, do not edit directly)
images/: Static image assets referenced in content
**_quarto.yml**: Global site configuration (navigation, theme, bibliography)
references.bib: BibTeX bibliography for academic citations
styles.css: Custom CSS overrides




The site uses Quarto’s website project type with: - Theme: Cosmo (Bootstrap-based) - Citations: IEEE style via CSL, referencing references.bib - Navigation: Top navbar with Home, Research, Teaching, Writing, About - Output: HTML with right-side TOC and smooth scrolling



Automated via GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/publish.yml): 1. Triggers on push to main branch 2. Sets up Quarto environment 3. Runs quarto render to build _site/ 4. Deploys to GitHub Pages






# Render the entire site (generates _site/)
quarto render

# Preview site with live reload (opens browser at http://localhost:4200)
quarto preview

# Render a single file
quarto render path/to/file.qmd






Create a new .qmd file in posts/ with naming: YYYY-MM-DD-title.qmd
Include frontmatter with at minimum:
---
title: "Post Title"
date: YYYY-MM-DD
categories: [category1, category2]
---
The post automatically appears in posts/index.qmd listing





Add BibTeX entry to references.bib
Reference in .qmd files using [@citation_key]
For nocite (show in bibliography without inline citation), use frontmatter:
nocite: |
  @citation_key1
  @citation_key2





# Check Quarto version
quarto --version

# Validate project configuration
quarto check

# Clean build artifacts
rm -rf _site/ .quarto/







All content pages use .qmd (Quarto Markdown) format
Frontmatter is YAML between --- delimiters
Posts must include title, date, and categories in frontmatter





Academic references stored in references.bib (BibTeX format)
Citation keys follow format: authorlastname_titleword_year
Use IEEE citation style (configured globally in _quarto.yml)





Store in images/ directory
Reference using relative paths: images/filename.ext
Use Quarto image syntax for captions: ![caption](path){options}






Do not manually edit _site/: This directory is auto-generated by quarto render
GitHub Actions handles deployment: No manual deployment steps needed after pushing to main
Quarto must be installed locally to build/preview the site (not present in current environment)
Bibliography changes: After editing references.bib, re-render affected pages to update citations
Post listing is automatic: The posts/index.qmd uses Quarto’s listing feature to auto-populate from post files

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text: This note details the derivation of a strong-conservation form of the enthalpy equation in terrain-following sigma coordinates. Our objective is to formulate the thermodynamics of an ice sheet in a manner that strictly conserves energy when discretized using a finite-volume method (FVM) on a dynamically deforming grid.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: Why Conservative Form Matters for FVM
text:
Why Conservative Form Matters for FVM
The finite-volume method is built around a simple balance law: the rate of change of a conserved quantity inside a control volume must equal the net flux through its boundary plus any source terms. In continuous form, that structure is
\[
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q.
\]
In a terrain-following sigma coordinate system,
\[
\sigma = \frac{z - b}{H},
\]
the computational grid stretches and shrinks as the ice thickness \(H\) evolves. If the enthalpy equation is solved in its usual advective form, the solver tracks the transport of specific enthalpy \(E\) but does not account for the changing physical volume of each cell. That creates a numerical mismatch: total energy can be created or destroyed when the ice thickens or thins.
To recover strict conservation, the natural finite-volume state variable is the depth-integrated enthalpy per unit area, \(HE\).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates

Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 8. Thermodynamic Boundary Conditions in Conservative Form
text:
8. Thermodynamic Boundary Conditions in Conservative Form
Because the state variable is now \(HE\), boundary conditions must be applied directly to the vertical fluxes rather than as pointwise constraints on \(E\).

Upper Surface Face (\(\sigma = 1\))
The total vertical flux \(F_\sigma = E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H}\partial_\sigma E\) has two components at the surface:

Advective flux: Using \(\omega_s = -\dot{a}\), the advective mass flux correctly injects enthalpy proportional to accumulation, resulting in a flux of \(-E_{\text{surface}} \dot{a}\).
Diffusive flux: A Dirichlet condition (\(E_s\) prescribed) implicitly determines the diffusive flux. The solver evaluates the gradient between the surface value and the first interior node, allowing the conductive flux to enter the sub-surface naturally through the diffusion stencil.



Lower Bed Face (\(\sigma = 0\))
In a standard advective formulation, the bed requires a Neumann condition for thermal diffusion: \(-\frac{\kappa}{H}(\partial_\sigma E)_0 = q_{\text{geo}} + q_{\text{fric}}\).
In conservative form, the total basal flux \(F_{\sigma, \text{bed}}\) automatically combines this diffusive contribution with the advective enthalpy loss caused by basal melting (\(E_b \omega_b = -E_b \dot{m}\)):
\[
F_{\sigma, \text{bed}} = -E_b \dot{m} + q_{\text{geo}} + q_{\text{fric}}
\]

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
Numerical Implications
For a finite-volume implementation, this formulation gives a few immediate benefits:

Internal fluxes telescope exactly, so flux leaving one cell is the same flux entering its neighbor.
The evolving cell thickness \(H\) is tied directly to the transported quantity, which improves consistency on a deforming mesh.
In the limit \(u = v = \omega = 0\), the equation reduces to
\[
\frac{\partial (HE)}{\partial t} = 0,
\]
so column energy is conserved even as the control volume changes.







Takeaway



If the mesh thickness evolves, a solver that advances \(E\) alone is not strictly conservative. Advancing \(HE\) instead makes the thermodynamics compatible with finite-volume mass conservation and yields boundary conditions that are naturally expressed as energy fluxes.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 1. The Cartesian Baseline and the “Flux Problem” in Sigma Space
text:
1. The Cartesian Baseline and the “Flux Problem” in Sigma Space
The finite-volume method is built around a simple balance law: the rate of change of a conserved quantity inside a control volume must equal the net flux crossing its boundaries plus any internal source terms.
In a rigid Cartesian coordinate system \((x, y, z)\), the physical volume of a grid cell is constant. Because ice is treated as incompressible (\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\)), the Cartesian enthalpy equation naturally exists in a strong conservative, flux-divergence form:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}_{\text{Cartesian}} = Q_{\text{Cartesian}}
\]
Here, the total flux vector \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{Cartesian}}\) combines both advective transport (energy carried by the moving ice) and diffusive transport (thermal conduction). Neglecting horizontal diffusion, this vector is:
\[
\mathbf{F}_{\text{Cartesian}} = \mathbf{v}E - \mathbf{q}_{\text{diff}} = \begin{bmatrix} uE \\ vE \\ wE - \kappa \frac{\partial E}{\partial z} \end{bmatrix}
\]
The source term \(Q_{\text{Cartesian}}\) contains only the true volumetric generation or destruction of heat strictly inside the cell—specifically, internal strain heating (\(\Phi\)) and meltwater drainage:
\[
Q_{\text{Cartesian}} = \frac{\Phi}{\rho} - \frac{\rho_w}{\rho} L \, r_d \, \varpi(E)
\]
(where \(\kappa\) is the effective thermal diffusivity, \(\rho\) is ice density, and \(\varpi\) is the water content).
However, in a terrain-following sigma coordinate system,
\[
\sigma = \frac{z - b}{H},
\]
the computational grid stretches and shrinks over time as the ice thickness \(H\) evolves. If the enthalpy equation is transformed directly into its advective form, we get:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}
+ u \frac{\partial E}{\partial x}
+ v \frac{\partial E}{\partial y}
+ \dot{\sigma} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
= \frac{\partial q_{\text{diff}, \sigma}}{\partial \sigma} + Q_{\sigma}
\]
This creates a severe numerical issue for FVM. While the spatial terms (\(u \frac{\partial E}{\partial x} + \dots\)) represent advective transport (\(\mathbf{v}_\sigma \cdot \nabla_\sigma E\)), they cannot be trivially rewritten as a flux divergence (\(\nabla_\sigma \cdot (\mathbf{v}_\sigma E)\)). In Cartesian space, we could pull the velocity inside the derivative because the velocity field is divergenceless. In sigma space, the effective “velocity” field \((u, v, \dot{\sigma})\) is not divergenceless because the physical grid is deforming over time and space.
Because the equation cannot be natively forced into a divergence form, you cannot apply the Divergence Theorem to calculate an exact boundary flux. If an FVM solver updates \(E\) using these advective terms while the mass-continuity solver independently shrinks the cell thickness \(H\), total energy is numerically destroyed.
To recover strict conservation, we must force the equation back into a flux-divergence form by shifting the state variable from specific enthalpy \(E\) to the depth-integrated enthalpy per unit area, \(HE\).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
Defining the FVM Face Fluxes
To implement this in a finite-volume solver, the equation must be expressed exactly as \(\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q\).
Because we unpacked \(S\) early on, we can explicitly separate the boundary-crossing transport terms (diffusion) from the purely internal generation terms (strain heating). By pulling the vertical diffusion component of \(HS\) over to the left-hand side, we define the complete total flux vector \(\mathbf{F}\) for the computational cell:
\[
\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_\sigma \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
HEu \\
HEv \\
E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The only remaining volumetric source term \(Q\) on the right-hand side is internal heat generation: \[
Q = \frac{H\Phi}{\rho}
\]

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
6. Transforming the Kinematic Boundary Conditions
Evaluating \(\omega\) at the domain boundaries clarifies this physical interpretation. The Cartesian kinematic boundary conditions for the surface (\(z = h_s = b + H\)) and bed (\(z = b\)) are respectively:
\[
w_s - \left( \frac{\partial h_s}{\partial t} + u_s \frac{\partial h_s}{\partial x} + v_s \frac{\partial h_s}{\partial y} \right) = -\dot{a}
\] \[
w_b - \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial t} + u_b \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + v_b \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} \right) = -\dot{m}
\]
Substituting \(\sigma = 1\) into our definition of \(\omega\) and expanding \(H = h_s - b\) reveals that all basal terms cancel, exactly matching the Cartesian surface boundary condition to yield \(\omega_s = -\dot{a}\). Similarly, substituting \(\sigma = 0\) removes the stretching terms, matching the basal boundary condition to yield \(\omega_b = -\dot{m}\).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 8. Conclusion: Why This is the Desired FVM Form
text:
8. Conclusion: Why This is the Desired FVM Form
We began this derivation by noting that a finite-volume solver requires the governing equation to take a strict flux-divergence form:
\[
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q_{\text{total}}
\]
The equation we have derived satisfies this requirement in the computational space \((x, y, \sigma)\):

The Conserved Variable (\(U\)): The state variable tracked by the solver is \(U = HE\).
The Total Flux Vector (\(\mathbf{F}\)): Every spatial derivative now wraps entirely around a boundary-crossing flux (combining advection and diffusion): \[
\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_\sigma \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
HEu \\
HEv \\
E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The Internal Sources (\(Q_{\text{total}}\)): The remaining terms on the right-hand side are strictly volumetric: \(Q_{\text{total}} = \frac{H\Phi}{\rho} - \frac{H\rho_w}{\rho} L \, r_d \, \varpi(E)\), representing strain heating and meltwater drainage.







Numerical Payoff



By moving the grid thickness \(H\) inside the derivatives, the computational grid \((\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta \sigma)\) becomes completely static from the perspective of the FVM solver. The Divergence Theorem can now be safely applied.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
5. Transforming the Continuity Equation
To proceed, we map the Cartesian statement of incompressibility (\(\partial_x u + \partial_y v + \partial_z w = 0\)) into sigma coordinates. Applying the multivariate chain rule to the horizontal derivatives accounts for the slopes of the constant-\(\sigma\) layers:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma}
\] \[
\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma}
\]
Substituting these alongside \(\partial_z w = \frac{1}{H} \partial_\sigma w\) into the Cartesian continuity equation, and multiplying the entire expression by \(H\) to clear the fractions, gives:
\[
H\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma + H\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma + \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) = 0
\]
Using the reverse product rule (\(H \partial_x u = \partial_x(Hu) - u \partial_x H\)), we force the horizontal terms into a flux-divergence form. Manually adding and subtracting the time derivative \(\partial_t H\) completes the mass conservation statement, allowing us to regroup the equation into two brackets:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{ \left[ \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y} \right] }_{\text{Divergence of Horizontal Mass}} &+ \\
\underbrace{ \left[ \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) - \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) \right] }_{\text{Geometric Residuals}} &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
This isolates a clean horizontal mass divergence, alongside a residual containing the vertical and geometric cross-terms. Notice that the second bracket is perfectly integrable with respect to \(\sigma\). We define a new variable, \(\omega\), such that its vertical derivative \(\partial_\sigma \omega\) is exactly equal to the residual bracket:
\[
\omega = w - \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} \right) - \sigma \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right)
\]
This substitution elegantly collapses the transformed continuity equation into its final sigma-space form:
\[
\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}
+ \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x}
+ \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y}
+ \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}
= 0
\]
Physically, \(\omega\) represents the scaled vertical velocity of the ice relative to the deforming computational grid, or \(H\dot{\sigma}\).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 4. The Emergence of Relative Vertical Velocity (\(\omega\))
text:
4. The Emergence of Relative Vertical Velocity (\(\omega\))
The algebraic transformation leaves us with a clean horizontal divergence, but a massive residual of vertical and geometric cross-terms.
However, if we look closely at that second bracket, it is perfectly integrable with respect to \(\sigma\). We can define a new variable, \(\omega\), such that its vertical derivative \(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}\) exactly equals that entire second bracket:
\[
\omega = w - \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} \right) - \sigma \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right)
\]
By making this substitution, the messy transformed continuity equation collapses into the sigma-space continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}
+ \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x}
+ \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y}
+ \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}
= 0
\]
While \(\omega\) emerges here as a mathematical necessity, it has a strict physical meaning: it is the scaled vertical velocity of the ice relative to the deforming computational grid (\(H\dot{\sigma}\)).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
4. Transforming the Continuity Equation
With the geometry derivatives defined, we can now transform the Cartesian continuity equation into sigma space using the multivariate chain rule.
A horizontal derivative taken at a constant Cartesian depth \(z\) must account for the crossing of sloped \(\sigma\) layers:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma}
\]
\[
\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_z = \left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma - \frac{1}{H} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma}
\]
The vertical derivative transforms simply as \(\frac{\partial w}{\partial z} = \frac{1}{H} \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma}\).
Substituting these into the Cartesian continuity equation and multiplying the entire expression by the ice thickness \(H\) to clear fractions yields:
\[
H\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_\sigma + H\left(\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}\right)_\sigma + \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) = 0
\]
To simplify this messy expression, we take the vertical derivative of our relative velocity equation (\(\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}\)). Because \(b\) and \(H\) do not depend on \(\sigma\), this derivative isolates the exact geometric cross-terms seen above:
\[
\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma} = \frac{\partial w}{\partial \sigma} - \frac{\partial u}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial x} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} \right) - \frac{\partial v}{\partial \sigma} \left( \frac{\partial b}{\partial y} + \sigma \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right) - \left( \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial H}{\partial x} + v \frac{\partial H}{\partial y} \right)
\]
Substituting this relationship back into our expanded continuity equation creates a massive cancellation, yielding the clean sigma-space continuity equation:
\[
\frac{\partial H}{\partial t}
+ \frac{\partial (Hu)}{\partial x}
+ \frac{\partial (Hv)}{\partial y}
+ \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \sigma}
= 0.
\]

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 1. Motivation: Compressible Flow, Variable Density, and the FVM
text:
1. Motivation: Compressible Flow, Variable Density, and the FVM

The Finite-Volume Requirement
The finite-volume method (FVM) is built around a strict physical balance law: the rate of change of a conserved quantity inside a control volume must equal the net flux crossing its boundaries plus any internal sources. Mathematically, this requires the governing PDE to be in strong conservation (flux-divergence) form:
\[
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q
\]
When written this way, the Divergence Theorem allows us to convert volume integrals into surface integrals. The flux \(\mathbf{F}\) crossing a shared face between two cells is evaluated exactly once—guaranteeing that every Joule of energy leaving one cell enters its neighbor. Summed over the domain, all internal fluxes perfectly cancel (telescope) to machine precision.


Why Specific Quantities Fail on Moving Grids
In a constant-density fluid on a fixed Cartesian grid, a specific quantity like enthalpy \(E\) satisfies its own conservation law trivially: \(\partial_t E + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{v}E) = S\). Because the grid is rigid and the flow is divergence-free (\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\)), FVM can be applied directly to \(E\).
The situation changes fundamentally on a deforming grid where the control volume changes size over time. Here, \(E\) only satisfies the advective (material derivative) equation:
\[
\frac{DE}{Dt} = \frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla E = S
\]
This is not in flux-divergence form. The spatial terms (\(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla E\)) are gradients, not divergences. You cannot apply the Divergence Theorem to them to compute a boundary flux. If an FVM solver updates \(E\) using these advective gradients while the cell volume independently shrinks or grows, the total \(HE\) in the domain will drift. Total energy is numerically destroyed.


The Ice-Sheet Analogy
This is a solved problem in compressible computational fluid dynamics (CFD). When gas density changes, aerodynamicists shift the state variable from a specific quantity \(\phi\) to a conserved (density-weighted) quantity \(\rho\phi\).
The depth-integrated ice sheet equations are structurally identical to the compressible Euler equations with a passive scalar. The ice thickness \(H\) (mass per unit area) plays the exact role of density \(\rho\) (mass per unit volume):







Compressible Flow
Depth-Integrated Ice




Density \(\rho\)
Ice thickness \(H\)


Specific scalar \(\phi\)
Specific enthalpy \(E\)


Mass flux \(\rho \mathbf{u}\)
Column mass flux \((Hu, Hv, \omega)\)


Continuity: \(\partial_t \rho + \nabla \cdot (\rho\mathbf{u}) = 0\)
\(\partial_t H + \partial_x(Hu) + \partial_y(Hv) + \partial_\sigma\omega = 0\)


Advective scalar: \(D\phi/Dt = S\)
\(DE/Dt = S\)


Conservative: \(\partial_t(\rho\phi) + \nabla \cdot(\rho\mathbf{u}\phi) = \rho S\)
\(\partial_t(HE) + \nabla \cdot(H\mathbf{u}E) = HS\)



The complication specific to glaciology is that our equations live in terrain-following sigma coordinates. But the core algebraic procedure to fix the FVM flux problem is identical to the compressible-flow playbook.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 8. Conclusion: The Deep Connection to Tracer Transport
text:
8. Conclusion: The Deep Connection to Tracer Transport
We began this derivation by noting that a finite-volume solver requires the governing equation to take a strict flux-divergence form (\(\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q\)). The equation we have derived perfectly satisfies this requirement:

The Conserved Variable (\(U\)): The state variable tracked by the solver is \(U = HE\).
The Flux Vector (\(\mathbf{F}\)): Every spatial derivative now wraps entirely around a boundary-crossing flux: \[
\mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} F_x \\ F_y \\ F_\sigma \end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
HEu \\
HEv \\
E\omega - \frac{\kappa}{H} \frac{\partial E}{\partial \sigma}
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The Source Term (\(Q\)): The remaining terms on the right-hand side are purely volumetric internal generation (\(Q = \frac{H\Phi}{\rho} - \frac{H\rho_w}{\rho} L \, r_d \, \varpi(E)\)).

By moving the grid thickness \(H\) inside the derivatives, the computational grid \((\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta \sigma)\) becomes completely static from the perspective of the FVM solver. Summed over the entire domain, all internal fluxes will perfectly telescope to machine precision, guaranteeing absolute global energy conservation regardless of how severely the ice deforms.
This formulation is not just a glaciology trick; it is the standard procedure used throughout compressible CFD and oceanography to transport specific scalars (like salinity or internal energy) on moving grids. This structural equivalence also dictates the correct numerical flux at the discrete level. Because \(E\) is a specific quantity carried by the mass flux \(Hu\), the numerical dissipation inside the FVM solver must act on \(E\) alone, not on the product \(HE\)—a requirement formalized by Abgrall (1996) to prevent thickness gradients from generating spurious phantom heat.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 1. Geometric Motivation: The Move to Sigma Coordinates
text:
1. Geometric Motivation: The Move to Sigma Coordinates
Ice sheets present a unique geometric challenge for numerical modeling. They are bounded by a complex, irregular basal topography (\(b\)) and a freely evolving upper surface (\(h_s\)).
If we attempt to model this system on a rigid Cartesian grid, these boundaries will arbitrarily intersect our computational cells. This introduces severe numerical complications, requiring either stair-stepped boundaries or fractional cut-cell tracking. Furthermore, because the most critical thermodynamic processes, such as extreme strain heating and phase transitions, occur in a thin boundary layer near the bed, a Cartesian grid struggles to provide adequate vertical resolution without wasting computational effort on empty space above the ice.
We resolve this by transforming the physical domain into terrain-following sigma coordinates:
\[
\sigma = \frac{z - b}{H}
\]
where \(H = h_s - b\) is the ice thickness. This mapping neatly abstracts the complex geometry, transforming the time-varying, irregular ice column into a static computational unit cube where \(\sigma \in [0, 1]\).

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 2. The Cartesian Baseline for an Incompressible Tracer
text:
2. The Cartesian Baseline for an Incompressible Tracer
To understand why this coordinate transformation complicates the thermodynamics, it helps to first review how a tracer is conserved in a standard Cartesian framework.
The finite-volume method requires governing PDEs to take a flux-divergence form (\(\partial_t U + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q\)). This allows the Divergence Theorem to convert volume integrals into surface fluxes, ensuring that energy leaving one cell enters its neighbor exactly.
The advective transport of specific enthalpy \(E\) following the fluid flow is given by the material derivative:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla E = S
\]
Because this equation relies on the spatial gradient of \(E\) rather than the divergence of a flux, it is not inherently conservative. However, glacier ice is treated as an incompressible fluid, meaning the velocity field is divergence-free:
\[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0
\]
We can multiply the continuity equation by \(E\) and add it to the advective equation without changing the physical balance:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla E + E(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) = S
\]
Applying the product rule groups the spatial terms, cleanly yielding the required flux-divergence form:
\[
\frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{v} E) = S
\]
In a fixed Cartesian grid, FVM can be applied directly to the specific enthalpy \(E\) because the incompressibility of the fluid guarantees that the transport terms perfectly balance.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 3. The Loss of Incompressibility in Sigma Space
text:
3. The Loss of Incompressibility in Sigma Space
When we map our equations into sigma space, the computational grid stretches and compresses over time as the ice thickness \(H\) evolves.
From the perspective of this deforming computational grid, the effective velocity field is no longer divergence-free. The geometric stretching of the grid acts as a local expansion or compression of the computational control volume. If we were to simply evaluate the advective equation in sigma coordinates and update \(E\) independently of these volume changes, total energy would not be conserved.
This situation is mathematically identical to modeling a compressible fluid on a fixed grid, where the fluid density varies. In our framework, the ice thickness \(H\) (mass per unit area) plays the exact role of density \(\rho\) (mass per unit volume).
To recover a strict conservation law, we must follow the standard procedure from compressible fluid dynamics: we shift the state variable from the specific quantity (\(E\)) to the density-weighted quantity (\(HE\)). The derivation below mirrors this procedure by transforming the continuity equation into sigma space and merging it with the advective enthalpy equation.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
text:
9. Conclusion
By conceptually treating our deforming ice column as a variable-density fluid, we have successfully cast the thermodynamics into a strict flux-divergence form: \[
\partial_t U + \nabla_\sigma \cdot \mathbf{F} = Q
\]






The Bridge to Discretization



The advantage of this variable-density framing becomes apparent when we move from continuous PDEs to discrete code. Because we have mapped the glaciological enthalpy problem onto the exact mathematical scaffolding of a compressible fluid carrying a specific tracer, we do not need to invent new numerical stabilization schemes from scratch. We can directly adopt proven finite-volume methods for existing problems.

title: Deriving the Conservative Enthalpy Equation in Sigma Coordinates
section: 3. The Compressible Analogy on a Deforming Grid
text:
3. The Compressible Analogy on a Deforming Grid
When we map our equations into sigma space, the computational grid stretches and compresses over time as the ice thickness \(H\) evolves.
From the perspective of this deforming computational grid, the effective velocity field is no longer divergence-free. The geometric stretching of the grid acts as a local expansion or compression of the computational control volume. If we were to evaluate the advective equation in sigma coordinates and update \(E\) independently of these volume changes, total energy would drift.
This situation is mathematically identical to modeling a variable-density fluid (like a compressible gas) on a fixed grid. In our framework, the ice thickness \(H\) (mass per unit area) plays the exact role of fluid density \(\rho\) (mass per unit volume).
In compressible fluid dynamics, there is a standard, mechanical procedure to recover a strict conservation law for any specific tracer \(\phi\). We shift the state variable from the specific quantity (\(\phi\)) to the density-weighted quantity (\(\rho\phi\)) using the following recipe:

Take the advective tracer equation and multiply it by the density \(\rho\).
Take the mass continuity equation and multiply it by the specific tracer \(\phi\).
Add the two equations together. The reverse product rule will perfectly collapse the advective gradients and divergences into a single conservative flux divergence: \(\partial_t(\rho\phi) + \nabla \cdot (\rho\mathbf{v}\phi)\).

The remainder of this note simply executes this exact mathematical recipe. We will define our advective enthalpy equation, rigorously derive our sigma-space continuity equation, and then blend them together.
